title: Commentary: Despite devastating floods, Nepal has limited options for climate compensation - CNA
description: Commentary: Despite devastating floods, Nepal has limited options for climate compensation  CNA
publisher.title: CNA
full_article:
NEW DELHI: Still reeling from the catastrophic glacial flood , Nepal has been struck again by flash floods that destroyed homes and infrastructure on Oct 11.

These back-to-back events highlight how vulnerable developing countries are to natural disasters, and how they bear the disproportionate brunt of climate change.

Nepalese authorities estimate that the August glacial flood incurred US$2.6 billion of property and infrastructure damage, and that reconstruction will cost US$4.8 billion.

Yet Nepal has requested only US$20 million from the United Nation’s Loss and Damage Fund – which is only about 0.4 cent of projected reconstruction costs.

title: Hundreds gather in Cary to raise money for Nepal disaster relief - Yahoo
description: Hundreds gather in Cary to raise money for Nepal disaster relief  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Nearly 400 people gathered at WakeMed Soccer Park in Cary on Sunday for a 5K race aimed at raising money for victims of catastrophic flooding and landslides in Nepal.

The event, organized by the Nepal Center of North Carolina, brought together hundreds of runners to support families affected by the disaster. Organizers said the local effort has already raised nearly $70,000 for flood relief, and the race is expected to add thousands more as recovery efforts continue.

For organizer Ashish Hara, the tragedy is personal.

"I was born in Nepal, and I came over to the States in 1988. So, I've been here a long time," Hara said.

He said one of his former classmates was among those affected by the disaster.

"During the floods, one of my classmates was an engineer in the hydro power station, and he was stuck in the tunnel. We never heard from him after that," Hara said.

The tunnel where his classmate was trapped was destroyed.

The flooding and landslides have left widespread devastation across Nepal, washing away communities and leaving families without homes, schools and access to basic necessities.

"These communities are completely washed away. There is no going back because billions of gallons of water traveled 100 kilometers, wiping everything out. People are buried under the mud," a race organizer said. "That place is not ready to build any infrastructure. It's like 10 feet of mud, and a lot of people and infrastructure are buried under it."

According to ABC News, the death toll has climbed to 1,287, with more than 5,000 people still unaccounted for.

Despite chilly conditions Sunday morning, hundreds of people participated in the event to raise both awareness and money for relief efforts. Organizers said the focus is shifting from rescue operations to rebuilding communities.

Dadin Pandey said support for disaster victims should transcend national boundaries.

"They need support, whether it's in-kind support or whatever you can donate, whatever way you can help."

The funds raised through the event will go toward helping flood victims and supporting rebuilding efforts in Nepal.

title: India not Bangladesh or Nepal - The Tribune
description: India not Bangladesh or Nepal  The Tribune
publisher.title: The Tribune
full_article:
Apropos of ‘How to unfurl the Tiranga’ (The Great Game); it is sad to see that leaders are using the Tricolour for political gains. Every political party worth its salt is wearing nationalism on its sleeve. By disallowing protests, the government is unwittingly increasing the pressure on GenZ. India has a deep-rooted democracy. India is not Bangladesh or Nepal, where student unrest changes regimes. A political change will take place only through elections. The government, on its part, should try to curb unemployment among the educated youth. Their grievances must be tackled through dialogue, democratic engagement and meaningful employment opportunities. However, this is not a permanent exemption. The Graham Act remains in force, and Washington retains the authority to reinstate the measures after reviewing Russian energy purchases. It is high time energy security was treated as a national security priority, not a commercial calculation. Bal Govind, Noida Avoid blanket access to AI Apropos of ‘Rogue AI agents’; an AI agent is no longer just a chatbot. It can read files, execute code, send emails, move money and change configurations. It must be ensured that no AI agent has blanket access. Agentic AI must get time-bound, task-specific and token-based access. Every high-impact action like deleting data, accessing financial records or sharing externally must require human-in-the-loop approval. Organisations must log every AI action like a financial ledger. AI labs must build agents with strong guardrails and kill switches. CERT-In has issued a warning. Now the regulator, the industry and the government must give the rules. Yash Khetarpal, Panchkula Make sound agri decisions Refer to ‘Protecting groundwater’; Punjab banned paddy sowing before mid-May and mid-June, aiming to make use of monsoon rains and reduce water consumption to 1,500-2,000 litres. However, the change created an unintended crisis: farmers were left with only 15 to 20 days between the paddy harvest and wheat sowing, making stubble burning the cheapest and quickest way to clear fields. As a result, a law intended to conserve water now worsens air pollution. As the Johl Committee suggested, shifting at least 20% of paddy land to maize, bajra, pulses and oilseeds is a viable solution. But alternative crops must be as profitable as paddy. Ultimately, protecting Punjab’s water and air will succeed only when moving away from paddy makes sound financial sense. title: Satellite Analysis of Nepal Flood Damage... Nara Space Steps In to Support Recovery - 아시아경제
description: Satellite Analysis of Nepal Flood Damage... Nara Space Steps In to Support Recovery  아시아경제
publisher.title: 아시아경제
full_article:
AI Estimates 31.28 Square Kilometers Affected by Flooding and Sediment

Building Damage Risk Areas Analyzed; Nine Priority Sites Selected for Field Surveys

Nara Space Technology, a South Korean space company, has used satellite imagery and artificial intelligence (AI) to assess the scale of flood damage in Nepal and support local disaster authorities' recovery efforts. By using satellite data to assess damage in areas that are difficult to access because of mountainous terrain and damaged roads, the company is providing baseline information for on-site surveys.

Nara Space said on October 19 that it had submitted a report analyzing flood damage in Nepal to the Embassy of Nepal in Korea. The report is expected to be forwarded through the embassy to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), where it may be used to assess damage and set recovery priorities.

Flood damage in Nepal's Nuwakot region, analyzed by Nara Space using satellite imagery. Courtesy of Nara Space. View original image

On August 26, a massive collapse of rock and glacial material in the Himalayan region along the Nepal-China border triggered debris flows and flooding. Soil and water flowed through the Lende Khola and Bhote Koshi rivers and spread downstream along the Trishuli River, damaging infrastructure including homes, roads, and bridges.

Using satellite imagery and its proprietary AI analysis technology, Nara Space estimated that about 31.28 square kilometers of land in the Trishuli River basin had been newly covered by water and sediment. An analysis using AI-based building detection technology found that the area where building footprints overlapped with the estimated flood and burial zones totaled about 52,180 square meters. Based on these findings, the company identified nine settlements in the Bidur area that require follow-up field surveys.

The analysis used Nara Space's AI-based satellite data analysis technology. The company operates EarthPaper, its proprietary platform that supports satellite image searches, disaster damage analysis, and report preparation.

"The value of satellite data lies not only in obtaining imagery, but also in turning it into information needed for real-world decision-making," said Kim Min-sik, head of business development at Nara Space. "We hope this report will help Nepal's disaster authorities assess the damage and develop recovery plans."

description: Nara Space maps Nepal flood damage with AI, flags nine sites for surveys - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz

full_article:
Flood damage in Bidur, Nepal, analyzed using satellite imagery and AI technology by Naraspace./Courtesy of Naraspace

Nara Space Technology (Nara Space) said on the 19th it delivered a report analyzing flood-affected areas in Nepal using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence (AI) technology to the Embassy of Nepal in Korea.

The report was produced to help assess the damage on the ground in Nepal and support recovery efforts. It is set to be delivered to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) through the Embassy of Nepal in Korea, and is expected to be used for damage assessment, field surveys, and reviewing recovery priorities.

A massive rock and glacier collapse that occurred on Aug. 26 in the Himalaya region along the Nepal-China border led to debris flows and flooding. The collapsed rock and glacier spread downstream through Lhende Khola and Bhote Koshi into the Trishuli River, damaging infrastructure including residential areas, roads, and bridges. In particular, in mountainous areas, road and bridge damage has limited on-site access, heightening the need to use satellite imagery for damage assessments.

Nara Space estimated the extent of the damage using satellite imagery and its in-house AI analysis technology. The analysis found that in the Trishuli River basin, the area newly covered by water and sediment is estimated at about 31.28 ㎢. The area where AI building-detection-identified building zones overlap with the estimated inundation/burial range was analyzed at about 52,180 ㎡. Based on this, it proposed nine settlements in the Bidur area as priority candidates for follow-up field surveys.

Kim Min-sik, Director General of business development at Nara Space, said, "The value of satellite data lies not only in obtaining imagery, but in turning it into information needed for real decision-making," and added, "We hope this report helps Nepal's disaster authorities assess the damage and draw up recovery plans."

Ghana’s Ambassador to China, Kojo Bonsu, has presented his Letters of Credence to the President of Nepal, Ram Chandra Paudel, at a ceremony at the Office of the President in Kathmandu.



Ambassador Bonsu, who is concurrently accredited to Nepal, conveyed the warm greetings of President John Dramani Mahama and the people of Ghana to the Government and people of Nepal.



He reaffirmed Ghana’s commitment to strengthening South-South cooperation and deepening bilateral relations between the two countries.



He noted the cultural similarities between Ghana and Nepal and commended the warm reception and rich ceremonial traditions of Nepal, including the ceremonial chariot ride to the Presidential Palace.



President Paudel, in receiving the credentials, commended Ambassador Bonsu for his dynamic engagement since assuming office in Beijing, particularly his outreach to the Ghanaian diaspora, drive for investment, and efforts to project Ghana’s image positively in Asia.

“We have already heard and read a lot of amazing things he has done and is doing. We follow his work with admiration,” President Paudel stated.



The Nepalese President expressed his Government’s readiness to deepen friendship with Ghana through cultural exchanges, socio-economic cooperation, and educational exchanges.

The ceremony, which marks a new chapter in Ghana-Nepal relations, ended with both sides expressing optimism for a future of mutual respect, friendship, and shared prosperity.

title: The festival season Nepal cannot celebrate like before - OnlineKhabar English News
description: The festival season Nepal cannot celebrate like before  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
More than 1.3 million people left Kathmandu Valley for last year’s Dashain alone. For a few days the capital empties out, and every road leading away fills up. In those same days, families buy and carry home close to 100,000 goats, a trade worth over three billion rupees. Homes stay lit for five nights of Tihar, enough to push the country’s electricity demand toward 1,300 megawatts. This is what an ordinary year looks like: people moving, money changing hands, lights in every window.

The rivers have not let up since August. The Bhote Koshi came first, into Rasuwa, after a glacier gave way above it. That water killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 more missing. It took down over 7,500 houses and upended 84,000 lives, more than a third of them children. The search was called off in early October. Five weeks later, it was the west’s turn. Twenty-one people died across Baglung, Myagdi, Palpa and Dhanusha. More than 1,500 lost their homes, and Manang and Mustang went dark.

Put those numbers side by side. In a fortnight, this country can move 1.3 million people across its own hills and trade three billion rupees in goats. It could not bring 5,285 of its own people home this year. Against the scale of the season, that number is small. To the families still waiting, it is everything.

It shows at Dashain first, which began on the eleventh and builds to Tika on the twenty-first. On the first day, Ghatasthapana, a family sows barley seed in a tray of sand. They set it somewhere dark in the house and water it for nine days. By the tenth the shoots come up pale and soft. They are cut and pressed onto the heads of everyone the family loves, with an elder’s blessing. It is a small ritual, and it asks for two people: one to sow the seed, one living to receive it. This year, in some houses, the one who would have sown the tray is among the missing. In others it is the one who would have knelt for the blessing. The tray may simply stay empty.

Tihar comes a fortnight later. Its best-known day, Bhai Tika, belongs to sisters and brothers. A sister strings a garland of Makhamali, the globe amaranth. It holds its colour long after it is cut. She puts it around her brother’s neck. The gesture repeats an old bargain: Yamaraj, death himself, agreed to spare a brother’s life as long as that garland kept its colour. Sisters do this every year without thinking of it as bargaining with death. This year, in homes across the flood-hit districts, there is no brother to put the garland on, and no one to strike the bargain with. The lamps that push the country’s power demand to its Tihar peak are meant to welcome people home. Some will burn this year for someone who did not come.

Then comes Chhath, kept at the river’s edge. On the third evening people stand waist-deep in the water and pray to the setting sun; on the fourth morning they come back to greet it rising. For families across Nepal it means wading into the same rivers that took a neighbour, a cousin, a friend this season. The sun will still set. The rite still calls them to the water.

The trays were meant to be sown on the morning of Ghatasthapana. The third river came down before dawn that same day. A landslide above the Budhi Gandaki seems to have dammed a tributary and then let go, carrying the water into Gorkha. Thirty-five to forty houses went at Jagat Bagar, Salleri and Ghattikhola. So did four bridges, among them the one at Arughat that ties Gorkha to Dhading, and the camp of the 341-megawatt Budhi Gandaki project. Helicopters worked through the day, and several people are still missing. It arrived on the morning Dashain began.

What Gorkha faces now, Rasuwa has been living with for six weeks. Nepal marked a national day of mourning on the seventh of September, the thirteenth day, when Hindu rites close mourning. Flags came to half-mast and the formal grieving ended on schedule. More than 14,500 children are still making up lost lessons. Most of the 4,500 who sheltered in tarpaulin camps now rent rooms around Bidur. The camps became unlivable, and the resettlement they were promised has still not come.

The festivals will arrive anyway, on schedule, as they always do. Households that lost nothing will keep them. So will households still waiting for word on someone who has not come home, often in the same village, sometimes the same street. The country holds both. What it owes the second has not changed since the water went down: rebuild their schools, their roads, their houses. And in a season built around who gets to come home, leave room for the ones who have not.

The villages still standing are owed something too. Each time, the warning started only once the water was moving, late for anyone near the top of it. Watching the slopes before they let go takes more eyes than one country keeps on a range this long. The families below them need more minutes than they are getting. A few minutes is not a large thing to ask the world for.

That kind of help takes years. Meanwhile Nepal has always been good at the quieter thing: standing close to each other when it is hard. Over the coming days people who waited months for a flight will touch this soil again. More than a few will walk into a house that is missing someone. The smile at that door may come a little unsure of itself this year. Nepalis have long known the harder kind of welcome anyway: sitting with someone’s grief without talking them out of it, and making room at the table whatever god a neighbour prays to, whatever language a guest greets them in.

Somewhere this season a family with little will cook enough for the family next door with less. A blanket will move from a house that can spare it to one that cannot, as it has in every hard winter this country has known. No report will record any of it. The hope is simple: that people find their feet with a hand on their shoulder, that they say the names of the ones they are missing out loud instead of alone, and that the hills hold so no one else has to be counted. Maybe they will find something in each other’s eyes brighter than any diya lit this Tihar.

None of that needs a ritual or an occasion. On a bus home this week, or in a courtyard strung with lights, a stranger’s eyes will hold someone else’s a moment longer than usual. It costs nothing to let that moment turn into a greeting with a smile. Whatever joy these festivals carry has always come from the people inside them, one smile at a time. This year, more than most, that smile is worth giving.

title: Police hunt Nepali links to 21.75 kg gold smuggling racket - The Kathmandu Post
description: Police hunt Nepali links to 21.75 kg gold smuggling racket  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Police are searching for Nepali accomplices in a suspected gold smuggling network after recovering 21.75 kg of gold earlier this month from a house in Budhanilkantha, Kathmandu, where three Chinese nationals allegedly operated a processing unit.

The Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office started its investigations regarding who helped store the gold, distribute it or transport it to India. Senior Superintendent of Police Santosh Khadka said investigators had yet to establish a Nepali connection.

“The three Chinese suspects have not cooperated much with the investigation, but we have sent the seized digital devices to a forensic laboratory, which may provide some information,” Khadka told Kantipur. “We are investigating other aspects as well.”

Police are questioning the suspects through an interpreter, but say they have answered a few questions. They are examining their contacts, devices, and CCTV footage, including airport parking footage. Police have not been able to identify the source of the gold or establish how it was brought into Nepal. Those questions remain central to the investigation.

Investigation officers believe that local contacts would be needed to store smuggled gold, distribute it, and send it across the border into India. Indian nationals may also have been involved.

Former Additional Inspector General of Police Basanta Lama, who served on a high-level gold investigation committee formed in 2017, said some Nepali involvement was likely. Even if the Chinese brought the gold into Nepal themselves, they could not take it to India without Nepali help,” said Lama.

Figures from the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association indicate that Nepal consumes around 30 kg gold daily, while Nepal Rastra Bank releases only 25 kg a day to the market through Rastriya Banijya Bank. That leaves an apparent shortfall of five kilogrammes.

“That gap is filled by smuggled gold; the rest of the gold brought in illegally goes to India,” said Lama. Police have not found evidence that Nepalis helped bring the gold into the country or prepare it for sale. They are investigating whether local contacts helped move it onwards.

A police officer said the Department of Customs was leading the inquiry, while police examined Nepali links and the suspected route to India.

Police arrested Chinese nationals Zhou Langqin, 47, Han Fei, 37, and Wang Jianzheng, 36, on October 8 after raiding a rented house in Bhangal, Budhanilkantha. The property belonged to a person living in the US. The suspects had rented it from July 23 and paid Rs1.32 million in advance for four months.

Investigators suspect the men chose a house whose landlord lived elsewhere, believing it would attract little attention. “They appear to have thought that nobody would pay attention if they rented a house whose owner was away,” an officer said. “Gold was brought there in a semi-solid form, processed and turned into bars.”

Acting on specific information, police had kept the house under surveillance for more than 10 days. There was little movement until a car left at around 5am one morning. Officers stopped and searched it, finding two gold biscuits. A subsequent search uncovered more gold and equipment used to process it.

GPS records show that the vehicle visited Tribhuvan International Airport’s parking area at least six times. Police suspect the gold may have been taken out of the airport in a semi-solid form before being processed at the house. Han had hired the car at the airport soon after arriving in Nepal, for use from October 10 to 25.

Police say Han had previously visited Nepal with his family on August 4 to assess the gold market and prices, returning to China on August 29. Investigators suspect he may have contacted Nepalis during that visit, although this has not been established.

“We have not found Nepali involvement in bringing the gold in or preparing it for the market,” said Khadka. “We are checking whether there were contacts involved in sending it to the market.”

The case follows major investigations that have not stopped gold smuggling in the country. Police data show that 579.218 kg gold smuggled by air and land were seized between fiscal years 2016-17 and 2025-26. During that period, 768 people were arrested, and Rs5.618 billion was recovered in revenue from seized gold.

One of Nepal’s biggest gold smuggling investigations followed the 2017 murder of carrier Sanam Shakya. The case exposed a network that brought gold from the UAE through Tribhuvan International Airport and sent it to India. Shakya was killed while the group tried to find 33 kg of missing gold.

The Home Ministry formed a high-level investigation committee led by then joint-secretary Ishwar Raj Paudel. It found that the same group had smuggled 3.8 tonnes of gold over four years. Cases were filed against 63 people in 2018. Lama said the inquiry exposed a network involving police officers, airport employees, carriers and alleged ringleaders.

In 2023, authorities seized 60 kg of gold concealed inside motorcycle brake shoes after it had passed through customs at Tribhuvan International Airport. The gold had arrived from Hong Kong and was intended for transport to India by road, investigators found.

title: Nepal to facilitate construction of 900 MW Upper Karnali hydropower plant — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS

full_article:
Nepal’s Investment Board has decided to facilitate the immediate start of construction of the 900 MW Upper Karnali hydropower plant in the west of the country. This was reported by the Kathmandu Post. The project, which had struggled for years to attract investment, is being developed by India’s GMR Group.

The decision was made at the 68th meeting of the Investment Board in accordance with the project development agreement. At the same time, the Investment Board Office has not yet sent GMR an official letter regarding the decision. The company said it would act after receiving the document.

Financing and shareholders

On January 15, 2025, GMR submitted documents on the project’s financial closure and said it had secured financing. According to the company, the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency, IREDA, gave a positive response to a proposal for a loan of 65 billion Indian rupees, while a consortium of Nepali banks preliminarily approved a loan of 20 billion Nepalese rupees.

Under the revised shareholding structure, GMR Group and India’s state-owned Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam each hold 34% of the project, IREDA holds 5%, and the Nepal Electricity Authority holds 27%. Previously, GMR held 73%, while the Nepal Electricity Authority owned the remaining 27%. GMR brought in IREDA and SJVN as shareholders to mobilize investment.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Deadlines and court proceedings

An expert committee under the Investment Board reviewed GMR’s report on financial closure and concluded that the company could have completed the process by the end of February 2025. A representative of the board’s office said that the developer may submit the remaining and updated documents and begin construction, which must be completed within the next five years.

In December 2024, lawyer Dan Bahadur Budha applied to Nepal’s Supreme Court. He argued that GMR had not achieved financial closure within two years after signing the agreement and had also entered into agreements to transfer stakes to other companies for investment in a project in India without government approval. The court dismissed the lawsuit and issued a directive order.

The full text of the court ruling states that the change in the shareholding structure did not require a negative attitude because it complied with the provisions of the project development agreement. GMR repeatedly received extensions to mobilize financing. The Supreme Court noted that the developer had already had 10 years to mobilize funds and prohibited any further extensions.

title: Nepal mourns: 'It hurts when the grandchildren ask for their parents' - The Star
description: Nepal mourns: 'It hurts when the grandchildren ask for their parents'  The Star
publisher.title: The Star
full_article:
More than a month since the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, many survivors are still struggling to comprehend what happened.

For 54-year-old Nepali mother Chameli Tamang, the pain and grief over the loss of her daughter, son-in-law and other relatives, who were swept away by the flood on Aug 26 and have been missing ever since, are overwhelming.

Her two grandchildren, aged five and eight, still do not know what happened to their parents.

“It hurts when the grandchildren ask for their parents.”

Tamang survived because she managed to escape to a mountainside in time. Nothing remains of her property in her home village of Sallitar in Bagmati province, which borders Tibet. Among other things, she ran a goat farm there.

“Now, we have no land and no home.”

Like Tamang, many families hope that the bodies of missing relatives will still be found so they can bury them and find emotional closure. Since the flood, they have spent their time “searching for them and lighting memorial candles for the dead in the monasteries”, Tamang says. “What are we supposed to do now?”

Nepal’s disaster management authority puts the death toll at more than 1,450.

However in Nepal alone, more than 5,700 people are still missing.

Nepalese authorities are already working on reconstruction efforts, but many survivors need psychological help.

Officials say the cause was an ice and rock avalanche about 20km upstream of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.

A mountain flank with a glacier in the border area between Nepal and China had collapsed, unleashing a massive flood wave of water, ice and debris. The affected districts were Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Chitwan, with a total population of 1.6 million.

Nepalese authorities are already working on reconstruction efforts, but many survivors need psychological help.

“Everything happened completely unexpectedly. Because of this and because of the scale of the disaster, people are in shock – they are distraught, restless and completely psychologically overwhelmed,” says Yasoda Rijal, who provides psychosocial counselling for people in emergency shelters in the municipality of Bidur.

Many are still suffering from severe psychological distress.

“As soon as someone talks about floods, streams, rivers or gorges, they panic.”

For some, post-traumatic stress disorders can also occur weeks after the event.

The communities therefore need long-term help. Authorities have drawn up a list of people who will need this in the long term, says Kaisang Nurpu Tamang, head of the Gosaikunda municipality in Rasuwa district.

“A month has passed, but there are still people who don’t even know where they are or what has happened to them.”

An aerial view shows the aftermath of severe flooding along the Bhotekoshi River in Nuwakot, Nepal.

People want certainty about their missing relatives. It would help them if they could be declared dead, says municipal head Tamang. The government has announced financial support for bereaved families, including for burial and mourning rituals.

Under current law, however, it is difficult in Nepal to have missing persons officially declared dead quickly.

Families and local authorities are therefore putting pressure on the central government to speed this up. (Editor’s note: On Oct 9, Nepal’s president shortened the waiting period to declare missing disaster victims dead from 12 years to 45 days.)

Clean-up work is under way. Many towns and roads are still covered with mud and rubble, and remote villages are in some cases still only accessible on foot. Reconstruction could take years.

“One month after the devastating floods swept through Nepal, thousands of families are still facing displacement, damaged services and uncertainty about what comes next,” the aid organisation Care said at the start of October.

The disaster represents an enormous economic burden for an already poor country, as was the case for the severe earthquake of 2015. According to an initial damage and needs analysis by the government, almost US$4.8bil (RM19.6bil) will be needed for recovery and reconstruction.

Damaged buildings and infrastructure along the swollen Trishuli River following the massive flash flood.

More than 7,500 buildings have been affected. Roads, bridges and energy and water networks have been severely damaged.

There are plans to rebuild destroyed villages in less vulnerable locations. The government is hoping for further international aid.

The government is now hoping for help from a UN fund for ­climate-related damage. Even before the flash flood, Nepal had applied for US$20mil (RM82mil).

Approval would be only a small part of the sum needed, but an important signal for the country.

After six months or a year, the problems could increase even further, says counsellor Yasoda Rijal.

Although some aid organisations are currently providing food and clothing, after six months the rice and lentils will be used up.

“For those who have lost relatives and their land, the need will then be even greater.” – dpa

title: Nepal Needs a River Corridor-Based Disaster Security and Incident Command System - myRepublica
description: Nepal Needs a River Corridor-Based Disaster Security and Incident Command System  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
The Himalayas are becoming increasingly vulnerable to cascading disasters. Rising atmospheric temperatures, glacier retreat, permafrost degradation and expanding glacial lakes are contributing to the destabilization of high mountain environments. Melamchi Flood (2021), Thame GLOF (2024), Bhotekoshi GLOF (2025) and now the recent disasters in the Bhotekoshi and Budhi Gandaki river systems have demonstrated how a sudden glacial collapse, rock–ice avalanche or landslide-dam breach can generate devastating floods and debris flows, threatening settlements, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream. Along with their increased frequency and intensity, its with urgent priority the action should be taken immediately.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

These events expose a fundamental gap in Nepal's disaster preparedness. While Himalayan hazards travel through interconnected river corridors, our emergency preparedness and response mechanisms remain largely organized around administrative boundaries. This conventional approach, primarily dependent on rain-induced disasters, is increasingly inadequate for disasters that originate in remote mountain catchments mainly triggered by ice-temperature dynamics and propagate rapidly across multiple municipalities and districts.

Nepal urgently needs a River Corridor-Based Disaster Security and Incident Command System across all snow-fed rivers with utmost urgency, led by the concerned National Authority, with the operational engagement of the frontline security forces; Armed Police Force, Nepal Police, Nepal Army, Department of Hydrology, Department of Meteorology, and provincial and local governments.

As Nepal's apex disaster risk reduction and management authority, NDRRMA should take responsibility for developing a National Himalayan River Corridor Emergency Preparedness Framework. Rather than establishing another parallel institution, this framework should strengthen existing disaster management structures through corridor-specific contingency planning, interagency coordination and operational readiness.

Based on the level of risk and the potential magnitude of hazards originating in the upper catchments, each major snow-fed river corridor should have a dedicated risk profile, a pre-established emergency response plan, clearly defined incident command arrangements, and designated multi-agency response task forces. Lead authority should coordinate these arrangements nationally, ensuring that scientific institutions, experts, security forces and local governments operate under clearly defined responsibilities and shared operational protocols.

Related story Revised interest rate corridor system introduced

Importantly, preparedness must be guided by the magnitude of potential disasters rather than historical experience alone. Scientific assessments should estimate the volume of potentially unstable glaciers, glacial lakes and rock–ice masses, together with possible flood discharge, debris entrainment, flow velocity and downstream impact.

The destructive potential of an event cannot be determined solely by the size of a glacial lake or collapsing glacier. Channel characteristics, sediment availability and valley confinement may substantially amplify its intensity. Therefore, corridor-specific hazard scenarios should determine where response forces are positioned, what equipment is required and how quickly evacuation must begin. This approach would not only strengthen preparedness and significantly reduce disaster-induced loss and damage, but also enable a more coordinated, timely, and effective response without requiring the full mobilization of central authorities and the entire government structure, unlike in the past. A dedicated corridor-specific task force should be sufficiently empowered to manage the initial response, with additional forces and resources mobilised as needed to provide targeted support.

From Reactive Rescue to Proactive Deployment

All three security forces have demonstrated considerable capacity in emergency rescue operations. However, responding after a high-velocity debris flow has already reached populated settlements may be too late. Under NDRRMA's national coordination, priority corridors should have designated emergency response teams, strategically pre-positioned equipment, evacuation routes, communication systems and operational command arrangements. A risk-tiered preparedness approach would be more practical than permanently deploying large numbers of security personnel along every river. High-risk corridors could maintain forward-positioned teams during critical periods, supported by mobile units and national reserves.

An effective Incident Command System should integrate scientific monitoring, early warning, security mobilization, evacuation, logistics and emergency communications. Clearly defined activation thresholds must allow authorized agencies to take immediate action without unnecessary administrative delays. Similarly, both Departments of Hydrology and Meteorology along with other technical institutions should coherently contribute scientific monitoring and hazard forecasts, while NDRRMA ensures that the resulting information is translated into preparedness decisions and coordinated operational action.

A National Priority Across Nepal's Himalayan Rivers

There must be a mechanism initiated for nationwide assessment of major snow-fed river corridors and their implications in each basin. The Bhotekoshi–Trishuli, Budhi Gandaki, Kali Gandaki, Seti Gandaki, Dudh Koshi, Tama Koshi, Sun Koshi, Arun, Marsyangdi and all other glacier-fed systems deserve particular attention, subject to vulnerability mapping along with scientific risk assessment and prioritization.

The immediate priority should be to identify the most vulnerable corridors, prepare scenario-based emergency plans, establish interagency incident command arrangements and conduct joint simulation exercises involving security forces, technical agencies and local communities.

Given the transboundary nature of several Himalayan watersheds, authority should also strengthen coordination with relevant national institutions for upstream hazard information exchange with neighbouring countries.

Nepal cannot prevent every glacier collapse, glacial lake outburst or catastrophic debris flow, given the frequency and intensity that are on the rise. But it can at least anticipate their potential consequences and prepare its institutions before disaster strikes. The time has come for NDRRMA to move beyond coordinating disaster response towards institutionalizing a proactive, scientifically informed and operationally prepared river corridor security system. The security forces, humanitarian agencies, international development partners and other responders must be integral to this mechanism, but its strategic direction, national coordination and accountability should rest firmly with the authority like NDRRMA.

The next major Himalayan disaster should not be the event that reminds Nepal of the need for preparedness. It should be the event for which Nepal is already prepared.

title: Nara Space uses satellites and AI to analyze flood damage in Nepal, steps up to support recovery - 매일경제

full_article:
Identify flooded and debris-affected areas using satellites Select 9 settlements urgently needing field surveys Deliver analysis report to Nepal’s disaster authorities

사진 확대 Ceremony at the Embassy of Nepal in South Korea to hand over a report analyzing flood damage. From left: Kalpana Bhandari, an official at the Embassy of Nepal in South Korea; Ghimire Ravi, sales manager at Nara Space; Nirmal Prasad Bhattarai, chargé d’affaires at the Embassy of Nepal in South Korea; Kim Min-sik, head of Nara Space’s Business Development Department; and Xenim Adhikari, second secretary at the embassy. (Nara Space)

South Korean space company Nara Space has analyzed flood-affected areas in Nepal using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence (AI) and has stepped in to support local recovery efforts.

Nara Space said on the 19th that it had delivered a report analyzing flood damage in Nepal to the Embassy of Nepal in South Korea. The report is to be passed on to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) and used to assess the damage and determine recovery priorities.

A large-scale rock and glacier collapse in the Himalayan region along the Nepal-China border on August 26 led to debris flows and flooding. As a result, residential areas and infrastructure, including roads and bridges, were damaged. Given the mountainous terrain, damage to roads and bridges makes it difficult to reach affected areas, increasing the need for satellite-based damage analysis.

Using satellite imagery and its own AI technology, Nara Space estimated that about 31.28 square kilometers in the Trishuli River basin had newly been covered by water and sediment. Its AI building-detection technology also identified about 52,180 square meters where building areas overlapped with areas estimated to have been flooded or buried. Based on this analysis, it selected 9 settlements in the Bidur area where follow-up field surveys are urgently needed.

The analysis used AI-based satellite data analysis technology developed in-house by Nara Space. The company handles everything from satellite design and manufacturing to operations and image analysis. title: How Nepal played a big role in South Africa’s liberation - The Kathmandu Post
description: How Nepal played a big role in South Africa’s liberation  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Anil Sooklal is South Africa’s High Commissioner to India, Bangladesh and Nepal. A career diplomat, he has served as his country’s ambassador to the European Union, Belgium and Luxembourg, and as its focal point for the Indian Ocean Rim Association. He was previously deputy director-general for Asia and the Middle East at South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation.

South Africa has no resident embassy in Kathmandu, so Sooklal travelled to Nepal during the festival season to meet the new government, the business community and civil society. He met with dignitaries including the foreign secretary, the ministers of foreign affairs, industry and tourism, and the Nepal Chamber of Commerce. Kantipur TV ’s Priya Sigdel sat down with him to discuss the two countries’ shared history, the aftermath of the Rasuwa flood, the role of honorary consuls and where the relationship could go next.

Why are you in Nepal at this time of year?

As High Commissioner, it is mandatory for me to come and engage with both the government and wider society. This is also a very special period for Nepali society. We have experienced the festival season in India, and we wanted to experience Nepal’s version of it as well.

Who have you met so far?

It was important for us to make contact with the new government. You have a new, young and dynamic leadership, and we were privileged to meet several ministers. We started with the foreign secretary, whom I know very well from his time as Nepal’s High Commissioner to South Africa. We then met the new foreign minister, the minister of industry and the minister of tourism, and we also met the leadership of the Nepal Chamber of Commerce.

What stood out?

The warmth with which I was received, and the genuine desire of the Nepali leadership to strengthen the relationship with South Africa.

Many Nepalis are hopeful about the new government. Are you?

I’m very positive. When you have change, you must embrace it. We embraced change in South Africa when we became a democracy, and we set about building the country. I think that is what the new leadership and the people of Nepal want: a better life for everyone.

What binds Nepal and South Africa historically?

What truly bonds us is the role Nepal played in our liberation struggle. Not many people realise that Nepal served on the UN Special Committee against Apartheid when it was formed in 1962. For 25 years, until 1994 when we became a democracy, Nepal was vice-chair of that committee.

The committee played a very important role at the United Nations in championing our freedom struggle and the call for South Africa’s liberation. So Nepal has played a very important role in our freedom.

How does that history shape relations today?

It forms a very strong basis for our bilateral relationship, and for the cooperation we enjoy at the multilateral level. We are both vibrant democracies, and we value the principles and ethics that govern democratic societies. We are also developing countries of the Global South, with similar challenges. Our people have similar aspirations.

Nepal recently suffered a devastating flood in Rasuwa. Was South Africa following the incident?

Very closely. Let me first repeat the condolences our government sent after the tragic event of 26 August. The entire world was shocked and empathised with this great tragedy. Just last week our press ran another story on it, because six South Africans are still missing.

Given the scale of the tragedy, it has a high profile in the South African media. South African society as a whole follows very closely what has transpired and the ongoing efforts.

Has Nepal kept you informed?

Yes. Despite the difficulties this tragedy has brought, you have constantly kept us informed about the missing South Africans and the efforts being made by the government and people of Nepal.

It speaks to the resilience of the people. Wherever we went during this visit, people were so positively disposed, with a very warm, welcoming disposition. That says a lot about the people of Nepal and about Nepal as a country.

What does the flood mean for cooperation on climate and disaster preparedness?

As countries of the Global South, we need to work more closely on climate change and climate action. What has happened here does not affect Nepal alone. It affects the entire globe, and we are all partly responsible. We are not keeping to the 1.5-degree target we set on global warming, and we are seeing the devastation this is having on our planet and our people.

We need to work together to enforce the decisions of the UNFCCC. More importantly, we need to contribute to the Green Climate Fund, so that countries of the Global South, Nepal included, can address the challenges of both mitigation and adaptation. Not enough is being done. This tragedy has brought sharp focus to the global community that we need to intensify our cooperation.

Could a disaster like this put foreign investors off? How can South Africa encourage investment despite it?

In our discussions with the ministers, we identified three or four critical areas where South Africa can play an important role. The first is reconstruction. Despite the tragedy, the destruction of infrastructure is also an opportunity, and South Africa is very strong in that sector.

The second is mining. We are a mining country with vast experience, and Nepal has vast, untapped resources. I believe South Africa can strengthen cooperation with Nepal in that area.

Third, you have a youthful, well-educated population, so there is great scope for cooperation in ICT and new technologies. We are also very strong in the agro-processing industry, and we can work closely with Nepal there. Green energy is another important area. The world is moving towards green energy and climate resilience, and South Africa has expertise to exchange with Nepal.

Despite South Africa’s strong global presence, few Nepalis know its shared history with Nepal. Why?

We need to put in greater effort on the visibility of the relationship, on both sides. We agreed on that during this visit. We need more exchange between our business communities and between the executive members of our governments.

What will change that?

I am very keen for some of our ministers to come to Nepal next year, and I am positive that will happen. We have invited every minister I met to visit South Africa. We would also like to see more people-to-people exchange, between our students, academics and business communities. We have been talking about this for some time.

We also met the mayor, and we have started an initiative to twin Kathmandu with Cape Town. You are the top of the world and we are the tip. From top to tip, it is a natural fit for creating synergies. I am positive that, following this visit, there will be concrete deliverables.

What kinds of South African business could Nepal attract?

There are three or four key areas we should focus on for mutual benefit. One is agriculture and agro-processing. Another is mining, including mining equipment, where South Africa is a leader. A third is infrastructure: you have major infrastructure needs, and we have very strong infrastructure companies, though we have our own needs too.

South Africa is also very rich in critical minerals, which is a global issue today, so we can look at cooperation in the mineral sector. And of course there is tourism. That is a natural fit as well.

How can the two countries create opportunities for students, young professionals and entrepreneurs?

In some of our discussions, we have talked about creating synergy between our business communities. The trade opportunities are vast. We saw some Nepali products, and I think there is a great market for them in South Africa. We are just not aware of it. Twinning business communities and chambers will provide that opening.

We know very little about each other, and yet we have this historical relationship. Once we create synergy through these kinds of interactions, there will be opportunities on both sides.

If you could take one concrete step today, what would it be?
